title: Node.js event loop
text: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single thread. The event loop takes callbacks from queues whenever the call stack is empty. Network and file I/O are handed to libuv and the operating system, so they do not block the thread. The loop has phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check (setImmediate) and close. process.nextTick callbacks run after the current operation, before the loop continues. Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always fires before setTimeout(fn, 0). Node suits I/O-bound servers, and CPU-heavy code blocks every request.

title: Streams and backpressure
text: Streams process data in chunks instead of loading a whole file into memory, which keeps memory use low for large files. Readable, Writable, Duplex and Transform are the stream types. Backpressure happens when a consumer is slower than the producer: write() returns false and the producer should wait for the drain event. The pipeline function connects streams, forwards errors and cleans up resources. Prefer pipeline over manual pipe for error handling.

title: CPU-bound work and memory leaks
text: To avoid blocking the event loop, move heavy computation to worker_threads, a child process, or a queue-backed worker service. The cluster module adds capacity across CPU cores but does not help a single blocked request. For memory leaks, monitor heap and RSS over time, take heap snapshots with --inspect or Chrome DevTools and compare them. Common causes are unbounded caches, event listeners that are never removed, timers holding closures, and global variables. Use bounded LRU caches or WeakMap, then verify under load.

title: Indexes and query plans
text: An index is a separate structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole collection. Indexes speed up reads but use storage and slow writes because every insert and update must maintain them. In MongoDB compound indexes follow the ESR rule: equality fields first, then sort fields, then range fields. A query can use any leading prefix of a compound index. explain('executionStats') shows IXSCAN versus COLLSCAN and compares keys examined with documents returned.

title: ACID transactions and SQL versus NoSQL
text: ACID means atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (valid state before and after), isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere) and durability (committed data survives a crash). A bank transfer needs the debit and credit to commit together. Relational databases excel at joins and multi-row transactions. MongoDB fits document-shaped data, flexible schemas and horizontal scaling. Choose based on access patterns, not fashion.

title: Sharding and shard keys
text: Sharding splits data across servers for horizontal scale. A good shard key has high cardinality, spreads writes evenly and lets most queries target one shard. Monotonically increasing keys such as timestamps or ObjectIds send all new writes to one hot shard; hashing the key spreads them but makes range queries scatter across shards. Ranged sharding supports range queries but risks hotspots. Changing a shard key later is expensive, so test with a realistic workload before committing.

title: REST methods and idempotency
text: REST models resources as URLs and uses stateless HTTP requests. GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces a whole resource, PATCH updates part of it and DELETE removes it. An idempotent request can be repeated with the same final state: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent while POST is not. Use status codes such as 200, 201, 400, 401, 404 and 429. For safe retries of non-idempotent actions like payments, accept a client-supplied idempotency key and store the first result.

title: JWT authentication
text: A JWT is a signed token containing claims. Use short-lived access tokens (minutes) and longer refresh tokens with rotation, so a stolen token expires quickly. Verify the signature and expiry on every request and always use HTTPS. Store tokens in httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies when possible, because localStorage is readable by any script and exposed to XSS. Keep a server-side way to revoke refresh tokens, for example by storing the current token hash per user.

title: Rate limiting
text: Rate limiting protects an API from abuse and overload. Common algorithms are the fixed window, sliding window and token bucket, which allows controlled bursts. Limit per API key or user and also per IP. With several servers, keep shared counters in Redis using atomic operations. When the limit is exceeded return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. Combine limits with timeouts and backoff on the client.
